# 1 Kinematics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Kinematics** is the branch of physics that **describes the motion of objects
without considering the forces that cause the motion**. These equations form the
foundation for more complex physics concepts.

## The constant-acceleration equations

The following describe the relationships between **velocity, position,
acceleration and time** for objects moving with **constant acceleration**.

**Final velocity**, relating final velocity to the initial velocity plus the
product of acceleration and time:

$$v = v_0 + at$$

**Position**, giving the position of an object based on its initial position,
initial velocity, time and acceleration:

$$x = x_0 + v_0t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$$

**Velocity–displacement relationship**, relating final velocity to initial
velocity and displacement **without requiring time**:

$$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0)$$

**Average velocity**, using the average of initial and final velocities to
calculate displacement:

$$x = x_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(v + v_0)t$$

## Where they apply

These equations are crucial for solving problems involving **motion in a straight
line** — free fall, projectile motion, and other scenarios where **acceleration is
constant**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kinematics** | The branch of physics describing motion without considering the forces causing it |
| **Constant acceleration** | The condition under which these four equations apply |

# 2 Dynamics: Forces and Newton's Laws

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Dynamics** is the study of **forces and their relationship to the motion of
objects**. Newton's laws of motion form the **cornerstone of classical mechanics**
and provide the framework for understanding how forces affect motion.

## Key formulas

**Newton's Second Law** — the net force acting on an object equals its mass
multiplied by its acceleration. The guide calls this **perhaps the most important
equation in classical mechanics**:

$$F_{\text{net}} = ma$$

**Weight** — the gravitational force exerted on an object by a massive body such
as Earth, equal to the product of mass and gravitational acceleration:

$$F_g = mg$$

**Friction** — the coefficient of friction multiplied by the normal force. This
applies to **both static and kinetic friction, though the coefficients differ**:

$$f = \mu N$$

## Other forces to understand conceptually

| Force | Description |
|---|---|
| **Tension** | Force transmitted through a string, rope, cable or wire |
| **Normal force** | The perpendicular force exerted by a surface |
| **Spring force** | The force exerted by a compressed or stretched spring |

## Method

When analysing physical systems it is crucial to **identify all forces acting on an
object**, **draw a free-body diagram**, and **apply Newton's Second Law** to
determine the resulting motion.

Remember that **forces are vector quantities**, having both magnitude and
direction — which is why the free-body diagram comes before the arithmetic.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dynamics** | The study of forces and their relationship to the motion of objects |
| **Newton's Second Law** | $F_{\text{net}} = ma$; the net force equals mass times acceleration |
| **Weight** | The gravitational force on an object, $F_g = mg$ |
| **Friction** | $f = \mu N$, the coefficient of friction times the normal force |
| **Tension** | Force transmitted through a string, rope, cable or wire |
| **Normal force** | The perpendicular force exerted by a surface |
| **Free-body diagram** | A diagram identifying all forces acting on an object |

# 3 Circular Motion and Gravitation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Circular motion** describes the movement of objects along a circular path, while
**gravitation** deals with the attractive force between masses. The two are closely
related, because **gravitational forces often cause circular orbital motions**.

## Centripetal force

When an object moves in a circular path it **constantly changes direction**, which
means it is **accelerating toward the centre of the circle**. That acceleration
requires a force — the **centripetal force**:

$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F_c$ | The centripetal force |
| $m$ | The mass of the object |
| $v$ | The **tangential** velocity of the object |
| $r$ | The radius of the circular path |

The reasoning matters as much as the formula: changing direction *is* acceleration,
even at constant speed, and acceleration requires a force.

## Gravitational force

**Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation** states that **every mass attracts every
other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely
proportional to the square of the distance between them**:

$$F_g = G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F_g$ | The gravitational force between the masses |
| $G$ | The gravitational constant, $6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg² |
| $m_1, m_2$ | The masses of the two objects |
| $r$ | The distance between the **centres** of the masses |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Centripetal force** | The force required to keep an object on a circular path, $F_c = mv^2/r$ |
| **Tangential velocity** | The velocity of an object along its circular path |
| **Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation** | Every mass attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance |
| **Gravitational constant ($G$)** | $6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg² |

# 4 Energy, Work and Power

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Energy** describes the **capacity to do work**. Understanding energy and its
various forms is crucial for analysing physical systems and their interactions.

## Kinetic energy

The energy an object possesses **due to its motion**:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$$

where $m$ is mass and $v$ is velocity. The equation shows that **kinetic energy
increases with the square of velocity**, making **speed much more significant than
mass** in determining an object's kinetic energy.

## Potential energy

**Potential energy** is **stored energy depending on an object's position or
configuration**. Two common forms:

**Gravitational potential energy** — the energy an object possesses due to its
height above a reference point:

$$PE = mgh$$

where $m$ is mass, $g$ gravitational acceleration and $h$ height.

**Elastic potential energy** — the energy stored in a stretched or compressed
spring:

$$PE_s = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$$

where $k$ is the spring constant and $x$ the displacement from equilibrium.

## Work and power

**Work** is the **energy transferred when a force moves an object**:

$$W = Fd\cos\theta$$

where $F$ is force, $d$ displacement, and $\theta$ the angle between the force and
displacement vectors.

**The work–energy theorem** — the net work done on an object equals its **change in
kinetic energy**:

$$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE$$

**Power** is the **rate at which work is done or energy is transferred**, measured
in **watts**:

$$P = \frac{W}{t} = Fv\cos\theta$$

Both forms of the power equation carry the same $\cos\theta$ as the work equation,
for the same reason: only the component of force along the motion does work.

## Conservation of energy

**Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to
another.** This principle is fundamental to solving many physics problems.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Energy** | The capacity to do work |
| **Kinetic energy** | Energy due to motion, $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ |
| **Potential energy** | Stored energy depending on position or configuration |
| **Gravitational potential energy** | $PE = mgh$, from height above a reference point |
| **Elastic potential energy** | $PE_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$, stored in a stretched or compressed spring |
| **Spring constant ($k$)** | The constant in the elastic potential energy formula |
| **Work** | Energy transferred when a force moves an object, $W = Fd\cos\theta$ |
| **Work–energy theorem** | Net work equals the change in kinetic energy |
| **Power** | The rate at which work is done, measured in watts |
| **Conservation of energy** | Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed |

# 5 Momentum

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Momentum** is a **vector quantity** representing the **product of an object's mass
and velocity**. It is **conserved in closed systems**, which makes it a powerful
tool for analysing collisions and interactions.

## Linear momentum

$$p = mv$$

Since velocity is a vector, **momentum is also a vector quantity** with both
magnitude and direction.

## Impulse

**Impulse** represents the **change in momentum**, equal to the force applied
multiplied by the time interval over which it acts:

$$J = Ft = \Delta p$$

This relationship, the **impulse–momentum theorem**, is particularly useful for
analysing collisions and impacts. It shows that **a small force applied for a long
time can produce the same change in momentum as a large force applied for a short
time**.

## Conservation of momentum

In a **closed system where no external forces act**, the total momentum before an
interaction equals the total momentum after it:

$$m_1v_1 + m_2v_2 = m_1v_1' + m_2v_2'$$

where the primed variables are the velocities after the interaction. This applies
to **collisions, explosions and other interactions** between objects.

Conservation of momentum **follows from Newton's laws of motion**, and it applies
**even where energy is not conserved** — as in **inelastic collisions**, where
kinetic energy is converted to other forms such as heat or sound.

That last point is what makes momentum more useful than energy for collision
problems: it holds in cases where an energy accounting would not close.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Momentum** | The vector product of an object's mass and velocity, $p = mv$ |
| **Impulse** | The change in momentum, $J = Ft = \Delta p$ |
| **Impulse–momentum theorem** | The relationship showing a small force over a long time equals a large force over a short time |
| **Conservation of momentum** | In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum is unchanged by an interaction |
| **Inelastic collision** | A collision in which kinetic energy is converted to heat or sound, though momentum is still conserved |

# 6 Rotational Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Rotational motion** deals with the movement of objects **around an axis**. Many
concepts from linear motion have **rotational analogues**, creating a parallel set
of equations and principles — which is the most efficient way to learn this topic.

| Linear | Rotational |
|---|---|
| Force $F$ | Torque $\tau$ |
| Mass $m$ | Rotational inertia $I$ |
| $F = ma$ | $\tau = I\alpha$ |
| $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ | $KE_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ |
| Momentum $p = mv$ | Angular momentum $L = I\omega$ |

## Torque

**Torque** is the **rotational equivalent of force**, causing objects to rotate:

$$\tau = rF\sin\theta$$

where $r$ is the distance from the rotation axis to the point where the force is
applied, $F$ is the force, and $\theta$ the angle between the force vector and the
position vector.

**Torque is maximised when the force is perpendicular to the position vector** —
that is, when $\sin\theta = 1$.

## Rotational inertia

**Rotational inertia ($I$)** is the **rotational equivalent of mass**, representing
an object's **resistance to changes in rotational motion**. Its value **depends on
the object's mass distribution relative to the axis of rotation** — which is the one
place the analogy with mass breaks down, since mass alone does not depend on where
you put the axis.

## Newton's Second Law for rotation

$$\tau = I\alpha$$

where $\tau$ is net torque, $I$ rotational inertia and $\alpha$ angular
acceleration.

## Rotational kinetic energy and angular momentum

**Rotational kinetic energy** — the energy of a rotating object, where $\omega$ is
angular velocity:

$$KE_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$

**Angular momentum** — a **conserved quantity in systems with no external
torques**:

$$L = I\omega$$

## Why it matters

Rotational motion is essential for analysing **wheels, gears, motors and celestial
bodies**. Conservation of angular momentum explains phenomena **from figure skating
spins to the stability of gyroscopes**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Torque ($\tau$)** | The rotational equivalent of force, $\tau = rF\sin\theta$, maximised when force is perpendicular to the position vector |
| **Rotational inertia ($I$)** | The rotational equivalent of mass, depending on mass distribution relative to the axis |
| **Angular acceleration ($\alpha$)** | The rotational analogue of acceleration, in $\tau = I\alpha$ |
| **Rotational kinetic energy** | $KE_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ |
| **Angular velocity ($\omega$)** | The rate of rotation |
| **Angular momentum ($L$)** | $L = I\omega$, conserved in systems with no external torques |

# 7 Fluid Dynamics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Fluid dynamics** studies the **behaviour of liquids and gases in motion**, with
applications in engineering, meteorology, oceanography and biology.

## Density and pressure

**Density** — the mass per unit volume of a substance, measured in kg/m³:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

**Pressure** — force per unit area, measured in **pascals**. In fluids, **pressure
acts in all directions**:

$$P = \frac{F}{A}$$

**Pressure at a depth** — the pressure at depth $h$ in a fluid, where $P_0$ is
typically atmospheric pressure, $\rho$ the fluid density and $g$ gravitational
acceleration:

$$P = P_0 + \rho gh$$

## Pascal's and Archimedes' principles

**Pascal's Principle** — in hydraulic systems, **pressure is transmitted equally
throughout a confined fluid**, allowing **force multiplication through area
differences**:

$$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$

**Archimedes' Principle** — an object immersed in a fluid experiences an **upward
buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced**:

$$F_b = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$$

## Fluid flow

**The continuity equation** — for **incompressible fluids**, the product of
cross-sectional area and fluid velocity remains constant. This represents
**conservation of mass**:

$$A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$$

**Bernoulli's equation** — representing **conservation of energy in fluid flow**:

$$P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$$

The two flow equations are the two conservation laws applied to a moving fluid:
continuity conserves mass, Bernoulli conserves energy.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Density ($\rho$)** | Mass per unit volume, measured in kg/m³ |
| **Pressure ($P$)** | Force per unit area, measured in pascals; in fluids it acts in all directions |
| **Pressure at depth** | $P = P_0 + \rho gh$ |
| **Pascal's Principle** | Pressure is transmitted equally through a confined fluid, allowing force multiplication |
| **Archimedes' Principle** | An immersed object experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced |
| **Buoyant force ($F_b$)** | $\rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$ |
| **Continuity equation** | $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$, representing conservation of mass in incompressible flow |
| **Bernoulli's equation** | $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$, representing conservation of energy in fluid flow |
